beats.narration_text: Six terms. An asset is a three-D model, image or sound a game uses. M C P, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard that lets an A. I. call another program's tools. A G L B is a single file that holds a three-D model. The origin is the point a three-D model is placed and rotated from. A triangle budget is the most triangles a three-D model may use. And last, a bounding box is the smallest upright box around a shape.

the smallest upright box around a shape

beats.narration_text: Simple has a precise meaning. Build each asset from Blender's basic shapes: cube, cylinder, cone, sphere, plane. Move them, scale them, combine them, give them a flat colour. No sculpting, no painted textures, no rigging, no animation.

After the midpoint they give way to the lantern's five clay parts, spread out and oversized, which slide and shrink into place (move, scale, combine); the real coloured lantern fades over them on 'flat colour' ('5 shapes, flat colours'). Four prohibition marks land beside 'sculpting', 'painted textures', 'rigging', 'animation'.

beats.narration_text: And there's a budget: no more than six basic shapes, and no more than five hundred triangles. A triangle is the flat, three-sided face every surface is cut into. Those limits keep everyone's work comparable. They aren't the engine's.

A cube wireframe (hidden edges dashed) draws; one triangle of its top face fills terracotta ('a triangle'); then a diagonal cuts every face (hidden ones dashed): 'cube: 12 triangles'. A brace under the numbers: 'course limits', then 'not engine limits'.

shot.visual_intent: A four-column ledger lands column by column: 'checked' (check mark), 'uncertain' (?), 'Claude got wrong' (cross), 'human / AI' (a person and a terracotta spark), each with two ghost lines to fill. Below, a real Blender screenshot (a viewport crop with the toolbar and the lantern, its base cropped off) lands and is labelled 'screenshot'; then the same lantern redrawn from its build numbers lands in an outline frame, labelled 'reconstruction'.
shot.motion_claim: Each column lands on its word; then the real capture gets its label, and the drawing gets the label 'reconstruction'.

lecture.runner_up: Remotion CCHumanLedger (two-column MUST/SHOULD ledger)
lecture.why: The assignment's film must state four separate things; four columns landing on four words beats a two-column human/AI ledger. The labelled pair (real capture vs drawn reconstruction) shows the labelling rule instead of saying it.

beats.act: VII · Ship It, and How It's Graded
beats.narration_text: Post the source to GitHub: the project, the three G L B files, the blend sources, the scripts, and your notes. Keep large media out. Tag the submitted commit a three, push the tag, and don't move it after you submit.

shot.visual_intent: A plain terminal (no Claude chrome) titled 'zsh — recorded output, example repository'. Real output of `git ls-files | column -c 66` in the film's example repository (22 tracked files in two columns: the notes, art/3d/*.blend, godot/assets/*.glb + .import, project.godot, showcase.tscn, the check script, tools/blender/build_*.py), then `$ git tag a3`. No path is shown.

show.event: rows stream in (11 rows, two columns)

shot.motion_claim: The tracked tree streams in while the voice lists what goes in the repository; the tag command lands last.

lecture.runner_up: Manim tree drawing of the repository with the real file names
lecture.why: git is a command-line tool: SHOW-THE-THING rung 1 is its real output. Constraints taken: CCPlainShell holds 13 visible lines (a 14th clips at the window edge), so the listing uses the real `column` formatting and `git log --oneline --decorate` is kept as evidence only (evidence/act7/b63_log_decorate.log); with one uniform line cadence every line lands before the 45 % window, so the tag line lands at 5.3 s, about 2 s before the voice says 'Tag' (11.9 s audio). 'push the tag' is not on screen: a separate `$ git push origin a3` line would be a 14th line, which clips at the window edge.

beats.narration_text: Then verify from a clean clone of the tag. Import once, run your check, open the scene. A working folder on your own machine isn't proof that everything was posted.

shot.visual_intent: The same terminal. The scratch path is replaced by the assignment's placeholder.

beats.narration_text: Grading. Sixty points for the work and its explanation, ten for your honest log, ten for matching versions on GitHub and Canvas, and twenty relative to the class. Meeting the criteria can earn the other eighty. It doesn't guarantee the twenty.

A brace closes over 60 + 10 + 10 with '80' and 'criteria met'; a terracotta ring closes round the 20.
shot.motion_claim: Each part grows as its points are spoken; the brace and '80' land on 'the other eighty'; the ring closes round the 20 on 'the twenty'.

beats.act: VII · Ship It, and How It's Graded
beats.narration_text: Late work loses ten percent a day. And you must be able to explain it. Be ready to open an asset in Blender and show where its size, origin and applied transforms are, and which part you edited by hand.

shot.visual_intent: Left: 'late work', a bar of ten cells loses its last cell (a dashed outline stays), '−10%' 'per day'; 'explain it'; then Blender's real icon with an arrow to two real crops of the Blender 5.1.2 sidebar (lantern selected): Location 0 m ×3, and Scale 1.000 ×3 + Dimensions 0.3 / 0.3 / 0.5 m. Terracotta rings close round Dimensions ('size'), Location ('origin') and Scale ('scale 1') on the spoken words.
shot.motion_claim: A tenth drops off the bar on 'ten percent a day'; the rings land on size, origin and applied scale as each is named.

lecture.runner_up: Remotion BrowserCapture-style push-in on the whole Blender window
lecture.why: The sentence names three fields of one real panel: real crops at 1.45x their pixels (type above the 4K floor) with one ring per spoken field show exactly where to point when asked. The whole window would put the fields under the type floor.

beats.act: VII · Ship It, and How It's Graded
beats.narration_text: One last point. A passing check shows your assets arrived at the size, orientation and scale you measured. It doesn't show they look right in your game. That judgment is yours.

shot.visual_intent: Two columns split by a rule. Left 'a check shows': size, orientation, scale, each getting an ink check on its word. Right 'only you judge': the real Godot showcase screenshot (look A, same crop as B61B) lands, then 'the look', then an eye with a terracotta pupil on 'That judgment is yours'.
shot.motion_claim: Three checks land on the three measured things; the right column has no check, only the real scene and an eye.

lecture.runner_up: Remotion LibraryIconRow (ruler, eye)
lecture.why: The claim is a contrast between what a check covers and what it cannot; two columns keep both on screen, and the right column shows the real scene the viewer must judge, not an icon of judging.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Three simple assets: basic shapes, under five hundred triangles. Learn Blender's window first, and name its six parts yourself. Write the brief before you build: size, origin, budget, predicted failures. Connect with the manual steps, mind the open socket, and fall back after two hours. Direct Claude one asset at a time, look yourself, and make one edit by hand. Check the numbers in Godot, judge the look with your own eyes, then ship.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I'm building a game that needs a simple three-D wooden crate. Help me write a brief for it: a size in metres, justified against my player's height, an origin at the centre of its base, a triangle budget of five hundred or less, and three predicted failures, each with the check that would catch it. Then write a short Blender Python script that builds the crate from basic shapes with no window, applies its transforms, and prints its dimensions and triangle count. Finally, tell me what that printout cannot prove. Then check two things yourself. Is the size justified against something in your game, and not just made up? And do the dimensions the script prints match the brief, with transforms applied?
